Georgy Zhukov. The Soviet Union's most celebrated military commander during World War II, serving as Chief of the General Staff and Marshal of the Soviet Union. His strategic brilliance in coordinating massive defensive operations and counteroffensives proved instrumental in turning the tide against Nazi Germany on the Eastern Front.

Zhukov rose from cavalry officer to become Stalin's principal military strategist, surviving the dictator's purges when many generals perished, and was appointed Chief of the General Staff in 1941. He impressed Stalin with his strategic insight and ability to implement large-scale operations across vast theaters of war. He orchestrated the defense at Stalingrad from 1942 to 1943, coordinating the Soviet counteroffensive Operation Uranus that encircled and destroyed the German Sixth Army and portions of the Fourth Panzer Army. At Stalingrad, he managed coordination between multiple Soviet army groups across hundreds of kilometers, demonstrating mastery of complex logistics and multi-front coordination.

He engineered the victory at Kursk in 1943, the largest tank battle in history, where Soviet intelligence and preparation defeated a German offensive called Operation Citadel. Soviet intelligence from the Lucy Ring spy network provided advance warning of German plans, allowing Zhukov to prepare massive defensive positions and counterattacks. He directed Operation Bagration in 1944, a coordinated offensive that liberated Belarus and destroyed German Army Group Center with over four hundred thousand casualties. Zhukov was a master of large-scale coordination, combining intelligence, reserve forces, and artillery concentration to overwhelm German defenses. He fell from favor after the war due to his growing prestige and Stalin's paranoia, though rehabilitated under Nikita Khrushchev and recognized as a hero of the Soviet Union. He died in 1974 and received a state funeral, cementing his legacy as the architect of Soviet victory.
